utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Toma Fila and I appear with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic in Defence of my client, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you follow me? Before we call the witness, may I ask you whether you agree to this note from the Registrar about the two documents which we discussed yesterday -- you have probably received the English translation of the bibliography of our witness, plus the missing pages of the other document, so I think it is agreed that they can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Shall we proceed with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we continue with our witness, I have a problem. We presented a motion today, to have permission for one safe conduct for another witness. I do apologise for this. I do not think there is any need for me to show how uncomfortable I feel about this, but I think that some of the witnesses told the other witnesses about their status with the safe conduct and (redacted), who is to appear on Monday, together with the witnesses, (redacted) probably discussed the matter with them and he is asking for safe conduct as well now. It is an important witness -- his importance can be seen from the fact that the Prosecutors talked to him for a long time, last night took a statement from him, and took part in the negotiations over Ilok and (redacted) one of the witnesses in this connection, he was the former President of the Municipal Assembly of Backa Palanka. (redacted) talked to this witness from Ilok. I think he is an important witness and can clarify matters around Ilok. I do apologise 5,000 times to you all, but it is out of my hands when the witnesses are in question. I think the Prosecutors can understand these difficulties, so I do ask you to give permission for safe conduct for this extra witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, we will have to consult with the Dutch authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may now proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Niemann, just one more moment. Tomorrow, they are to be granted visas, all the witnesses and nobody has visas as yet, neither do they have aeroplane tickets. You know, you live in countries where you do not need visas, whereas, with us, this is a great problem. So, I should like to ask you, if you could, speed up with the contacts with the Dutch police. If they do not obtain a visa by tomorrow afternoon, that is by Thursday afternoon, they have to have visas by 9 on Friday. Thank you. I apologise, Mr. Niemann, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Registrar can tell us whether measures can be put in place, so that the necessary visas are provided?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will be able to arrange that. I will talk this morning with the relevant people at the Registry, but I do not think that it should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann -- I wonder whether the witness could be brought in. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: ZLATIJE DJUKIC-VELJKOVIC (continued).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday you were speaking of the Constitution of 1974 and explaining to the court how you had undertaken a special study in that area. Professor, under the 1974 Constitution, I think there is a provision there, is there not, that President Tito was to be President for life prior to the operation of the rotating presidency; is that right -- no translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can I repeat the question for you, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, would you repeat the question, please, because there was something wrong with the earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means. Is it true that, under the 1974 Constitution, Tito was appointed President for life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you still having problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Translation -- excuse me, pardon. Yes, I can hear now, thank you. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will repeat the question again and see if we can get it this time. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I should say that if you have any difficulty understanding anything I say, or hearing me, please do not hesitate to let me know so that we can clear that up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was asking you, was it true that, under the 1974 Constitution, Tito was appointed President for life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually, we say that he was Josip Broz Tito, was nominated President for life and my students usually answer, when I ask them, that, according to the Constitution of 1974, he was proclaimed life President. However, if we are to be precise legally, and constitutionally, he was not appointed life-long President on the basis of the constitution, but was given the possibility of being elected by the Assembly, the Federal Assembly, under whose competence this was, without any limitation of tenure. For other appointments, according to this constitution, and for that period, there was a restriction in the term of office, but for Josip Broz Tito this did not hold true, but he was given the possibility of being elected any number of times, an unrestricted number of times, as President of Yugoslavia. So, to be precise, nowhere in the constitution did the norm exist, a formula exist, that Josip Broz Tito is the life-long President of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but on the basis of the will of the people and the people's representatives in the assemblies, both republican and provincial, that he can be proposed to be elected for an unrestricted number of times by the Federal Parliament as President of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me, would you not, Professor, that the effect of this was that the rotating presidency, if I can use that perhaps crude language, did not come into effect until after his death, that is, Tito's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but let me add something here. By the constitution itself and the constitutional amendments in 1971, so the amendments started before the actual 1974 Constitution, the amendments to the previous constitution and the supplements to the constitution introduced the presidency of the SFRY as a collective head of State for the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, -- in that, the same amendments provided for the fact that, while Josip Broz Tito performs the function of the President of the SFRY, the presidency of the SFRY, or let me say this in simple terms -- the presidency was the potential organ which would automatically come on the scene at the precise moment when Josip Broz Tito ceases to perform his function as President. We cannot say -- we did not say by virtue of his death, because there was the theoretical possibility of Josip Broz Tito tendering his resignation or ceasing to be President in some other manner and that is when the constitutional amendments would come into play, and the presidency, as a collective head of State, would take over the function of the Head of State of the Common State.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, in reality, the experience of having a rotating presidency was not something familiar to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia until after Tito died -- you would agree with that, I think, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday, I think we understood one another very well. I am speaking about the constitutional model, on the one hand, and what is provided for on the basis of norms, and what we constitutionalists always have to bear in mind -- there are norms and I adhere to those norms because the constitution of the lex superior, the highest law of the country, whereas in practice things were sometimes different. I know that as a citizen of Yugoslavia and as an expert as well, the situation was somewhat different, but that is another dimension of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At various times yesterday in your evidence, Professor, you spoke of the sovereignty of the State. You may not have used those terms, but we were talking about Croatia and other republics. What criteria do you yourself apply when it comes to determining what constitutes independent sovereignty of the State -- what are the criteria that you apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about this, and I used the term "sovereignty", because when we are talking about a federally organised State, then the first and classical constitutional right is a theoretical question as to who has sovereignty in the State -- in a State which has two levels of power, one is central power and the second level is the power and authority of the Federal units. Since the first Federal State was introduced, that is to say, the United States of America, I think this question is common knowledge, that is, we know who is sovereign, but this was a pivotal question, and theory had to deal with that question. It was a stumbling block and the secessionist war in the second half of the last century in the federation, which is well known as the first federation, and a stable federation which has been going on for the past two centuries and theory gave its answer and I think that is the only possible answer, that the vehicle of sovereignty in Yugoslavia is the Federal State, that is to say, the first level I mentioned a moment ago, whereas the criterion for sovereignty is the one that the power and authority in the federation has two meanings. It is the highest authority, both internally and externally and in a synthetic meaning which comprises the two, that is to say, the power and authority of the federation is embodied in its top most organs determined by lex superior is the highest authority in the territory of the State. All other authorities of the Federal units are subordinate to the Federal authority and that is the second feature of sovereignty. Am I answering your question? I think I am. And that is sovereignty in comparison to other States and this synthetic third element, this top power, the federation, which is the emanation of supreme power and authority both internally and externally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think perhaps I was asking a more general question, and you were sort of answering it in the context more of a federation, but would you agree with me -- perhaps we can come at it this way -- that it is generally established that some of the criteria that are applied to determine sovereignty is firstly territory, then that there is a functioning Government and then that there is population -- at least those three criteria -- would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think that your question, in fact, follows on from what I said a moment ago and your first question and these are the properties of the State -- the conditions to be fulfilled for a State to be recognised as a State. Those are the three necessary criteria you must fulfil -- territory, the population and functional Government. Is that a more precise answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we agree that this is connected to what was said about the federation earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I do not want in any way to discourage you from expanding upon your answers and, if you think it is necessary to give a detailed answer to fairly answer my questions, please do not hesitate to do so, but a lot of my questions probably only require a "Yes" or "No" answer, so if you feel that you can answer the question that I am putting to you with a "Yes" or "No" answer, do not feel in any way obliged to have to go into a detailed explanation, so it is a matter entirely for you and I do not want to interfere with the way you address the issues I put to you, but if you feel you can answer it with a "Yes" or "No", please feel free to do so. Immediately after saying that, the next question will require an explanation, I think. You speak of this notion of citizenship of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and citizenship in a republic itself and you say that, if you lose the citizenship of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then you automatically lose the citizenship of the Republic. Am I right in saying that -- is that what you said -- is that a fair statement of your views on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for warning me to be succinct and give "Yes" or "No" answers, but I would just like to tell you that I am here as an expert for constitutional law, so you will be helping me if you guide me towards answering the questions as you would have them answered. I shall be very grateful to you for that. Now, to get back to the concrete question. As far as citizenship is concerned, I think we understand each other. I am talking about the constitutional provisions, about citizenship in a Federal State. These provisions are not the characteristic only of the constitution of a Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that we are discussing now, but they are also provisions which are characteristic more or less in different formulations for the constitution of the majority of federally organised States. Therefore, it means Federal citizenship, citizenship of a federation -- it is a category which implements the citizenship of the Federal unit and in conformity with this, and that is characteristic with other federations as well, as I said yesterday, that in Yugoslavia as well, there is Republican citizenship, there is Federal citizenship as determined by the constitution, and in keeping with the constitution and Federal laws and Republican laws on citizenship, it is true, Sir, that I said that Republican citizenship cannot exist without Federal citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite simply, the federation is a Federal State. It is a State which is composed of Federal units, and it is an essentially different category from an alliance, a confederation of States and one of the characteristics of a Federal State is precisely the fact that it has citizenship -- the citizenship of its citizens -- dual citizenship, as I say -- the citizenship of the Federal unit and, on that basis, citizens gain the right to citizenship of the alliance cities, a legal link between the citizens of a Federal State because we are talking about a Federal State, I would like to underline that, and not a confederation, so it is the legal links between the citizens and their Federal State as a united unique State -- specific of course, if we compare it to a unitarian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does that not mean that one works hand in hand with the other, so that it does not matter either way? If you have a Federal unit, and the federation breaks down, that has an impact upon the remaining States and, conversely, if the States take matters into their own hands, that also has a converse effect, does it not? So, it is not true to say it only works one way; in other words, if you lose citizenship of a republic, then that has the same effect as if you lose citizenship of the SFRY, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I understand your question, but I should like to ask you to clarify it, if you would, because I have stated on the disintegration of the Federal State and that is something else, so would you clarify your question? We are talking about a State which exists, which has not disintegrated, and the position of its citizens, living in the Federal units and in that sense they should be protected and have links with the Federal unit, and they are citizens of the Federal State. So, I think we should clarify matters on that point. I am not talking about the situation where there is a disintegration of the State -- that is not in my domain. I am an expert on the Federal State as an authentic form of statehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Quite so, and I will endeavour to clarify the issue for you. You have said that your testimony relates to the existence and the continued existence of the Socialist Federal Republic, but you also, at the same time, speak about the issue of citizenship and what impact the loss of Federal citizenship would have on a particular Republican citizenship -- I think we have established that if one goes, the other goes. The point I am trying to make, though, is that a federation is just not a one way street -- it works both ways. It is the States to Federal Government and the Federal Government back down to the States. It is not just one way. The point I make is that there is no difference between losing Federal citizenship than losing Republican citizenship in the sense that one must go hand in hand with the other. Must you not have both to function effectively and properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For it to function as it should function, we have Republican citizenship in the federation which exists and the Federal citizenship and, on both counts, we gain the corresponding rights, duties and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely. So, the law concerning the implementation of the constitutional law for the autonomous district of Slovenia, Banija and Western Srem of 13 August 1991, we looked at, and, in particular, in relation to the law where the decision of 30 August was implemented, article 4 of that particular provision speaks of the fact that the inhabitants of the Serb district, presumably in Croatia -- although it does not say so but it is logical that it must be -- shall cease to be citizens of the Republic of Croatia, retaining their citizenship of Yugoslavia. On your theory, that cannot be right, can it, as a matter of law?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I give this document to the Prosecutor? It might clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to be clearer in my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is Defence D16. Mr. Niemann is quoting the document D16, and can we have this document handed to the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Mr. Fila is asking for the document to be given to the witness, by all means, but I thought she could ask for it herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I quote anything to you and you want to look at the document, please do not hesitate to ask for it. (Handed). What article did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Article 4. I thought it was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The law on the implementation of the constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: D16A, article 4 -- do you see that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not in contradiction with what I said yesterday. Yesterday, we said, did we not, that Republican citizenship cannot exist without Federal citizenship and that is the point, and here we are talking about a provisional law, which was enacted for separate reasons which I do not want to go into now, but the point of this article is, and I should like to draw your attention to that, that, for citizenship of -- it is about Yugoslav citizenship and that is the thesis that, by losing Republican citizenship, -- the point is, in citizenship of a Federal State, and that you cannot have the existence of Republican citizenship without Federal citizenship, so I do not consider that there is a collision here in regard to what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you would say that a provision which deprives a citizen of the Republic of Croatia of citizenship, such as article 4 does, is a constitutionally valid provision under the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that your position on the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that this provision is valid, but I wish to draw your attention to the following: there is something that one should not lose sight of here and that is the major fact that the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, from 1990, in that Constitution the Serbs were no longer a constituent people of the Republic of Croatia, so this has to be viewed in that context. This major historic mistake that was made then, and I wish to draw your attention to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking you to justify it, professor. I am merely asking you to comment upon the legality of it, and I am saying to you, surely you are not seriously suggesting that article 4 conforms with the 1974 Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, Sir, but may I be allowed to say that I believe that the relevant fact here is that the Serb people -- I am sorry to have to insist on this -- but the Serb people were turned into a national minority by the 1990 Constitution. I wish to draw your attention to an injustice that was done by the international community and that is this solution found in the 1990 Constitution and what I would consider to be valid is the fact that the international community did not support this. In fact, on several occasions the international community reacted to this as to a solution which was not supposed to be part of the then constitution and, sorry, Mr. Niemann, but that is why I insisted on this. I wanted to corroborate it. I do not want this to be -- this was not in contravention to the then valid constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Constitutional Court consider this provision, this law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why not -- it impacted upon the Federal constitution, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The provision of this law -- this provision? There was no-one who thought that this provision was not in line with the constitution, that is, those provisions that we quoted yesterday on Federal citizenship and citizenship of the Federal units. There were no initiatives and no proposals to this effect and the Constitutional Court itself, at its own initiative did not start a procedure, so this provision remained as a valid provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This provision, in part, impacts upon the territorial borders of Croatia, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand this. In what sense -- the territorial border with Croatia? Why would this be impacted, because the two should not be linked. Really, from the point of view of constitutional law, I do not see a link between these two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can explain it a little better, then. We have here a law, which purports to deal with Croat citizenship in the territory of Croatia, and we have here a law, which purports to effect Croat law on its own territory, do we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, are you referring to the same law?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes -- exhibit D16 which you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of this is within the framework of the then valid constitution of the SFRY, and therefore I would not link these two matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I proceed from the following -- sorry, Sir -- but I proceed from the following: we are talking about the SFRY constitution which is still valid and Federal laws that were still valid at that time, and Republican laws, too, and it is in that context that we have to move -- I have to move in that context in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. So you are suggesting that the Federal law would supersede and prevail over the laws of a republic and laws of this Serb district -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with that, because this is a basic tenet in any Federal State, but it is also true that here I do not believe there is a collision in this sense -- there is, on the one hand, the valid constitution of the SFRY; there are the constitutions of the republics that are still in force; there is the Federal legislation which is above Republican legislation and above all other acts; and within this framework we are assessing as to whether these acts have been brought into line with one another or not. From the point of view of what I said yesterday, there is no lack of concordance here, and this was also confirmed by the Constitutional Court in terms of the hierarchy of the legal order in Yugoslavia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, you would seriously suggest to the Tribunal that it would be perfectly in accord with the Federal law and the law of Yugoslavia as it then applied, for the law of the Republic of Serbia to be applied and operate and be effective in the Republic of Croatia; are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about special circumstances, but the key fact for me here is that, in that period, the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in force. The Federal laws were still in force, and, in that context, we assess all other acts that are adopted after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Article 2 of exhibit 16 is a curious provision, is it not, Professor? What do we have here? We have that the Federal law shall apply so long as it is not in conflict with the legislation of the district, which would seem to be contrary to what you said a moment ago, and it also says that the legislation of the Republic of Serbia will start being applied to territory which is covered by this provision, which includes territory of Croatia, and yet you assert that this is a constitutionally valid provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood this correctly -- actually, I would prefer a more concise question, if this is not too difficult for you now. What is the point that you are making on the basis of all of this so we can be precise as possible? I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sure. You were telling me a moment ago how you considered this particular provision, exhibit 16, to be a constitutionally valid provision under the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974. You were telling me that and you are asserting that. You then also told me that the Federal law would prevail over the laws of the Republic, because that is the nature of a federation, and you did not say, but I assume you surely would not disagree, that there is nowhere in the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974 which permits the law of one republic to prevail and operate and apply on the territory of another republic -- you do not argue with that, do you, surely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, let us bear in mind the fact that we are not talking about the law of a new republic, because the Serb district is not a new republic. We have to bear in mind the entire context. We are talking about a provisional arrangement, and we have to take into account the broader circumstances in which the Serb district was in that situation, and given the events that were taking place. So I wish to say that I do not consider this question to be all that important from the point of view of the situation in general, and from the point of view of constitutionality and legality -- in its legal meaning. It is not that a new republic was established here on the territory of another republic; there is a federation, so what we have now is a situation in which, on one part of the territory, which is under Serb control, a district is constituted and it is proclaiming its organisation to be a provisional one and I must add that the international community was participating in this throughout, and all of this was under a certain degree of control, with the best of intentions, that is to get out of the crisis in which the federation was then, as well as its constituent parts. So, I do not think it is important now, from the point of view of constitutionality and legality, and from another point of view, to dwell on this subject much longer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The important thing -- sorry -- the important thing is that the constitutional provision on citizenship of the SFRY remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, far more important is the fact that the Serbs were unconstitutionally erased from the constitution in 1990 and this was condemned by the international community. The international community did not accept this, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking you, Professor, to tell us the justification or rationale behind it. It could be perfectly valid and very appropriate, but I am not asking you that. I am asking you questions about the operation of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the impact of these laws -- those are my questions, but I will move on. This law, this exhibit 16, speaks of a "Great National Assembly". What is that and, in particular, your Honours, Article 2 of exhibit 16 mentions that. What is "the Great National Assembly"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I mention in passing that I have not come here to defend certain solutions or attack others. I am here exclusively as a Professor of Constitutional Law and I wish to assist in this matter, and I think that this is the most important thing that we are trying to do, to get a real picture of the events that were taking place. Actually, I am a Professor of Constitutional Law, so I am talking about normative models, so I would not wish to get out of this framework, nor do I think that it would really be good for the ultimate objective. I repeat: we are talking about provisional arrangements in a special situation, and efforts that are made in a normative fashion to get out of that crisis in the best way possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the answer to my question, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that is why we are talking about Article 2, the Great Assembly, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a provisional organisation and it has its genesis and I elaborated on that in my expert opinion. Sorry, the question: could you spell it out more precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked you a very simple question. What is the Great National Assembly? If you do not know, please say so -- "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Great National Assembly is an organ which was envisaged to be one of the organs functioning on that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What was the word "national", what did that mean? What did that apply to in that term "the Great National Assembly"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We referred to all assemblies as national, as peoples' assemblies. This was meant to show that these were democratic institutions, that it was the people who were represented there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Great National Assembly -- the people who were negated in that area -- the people who were in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that the Serbs, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the territory that was under Serb control, and they constituted their provisional Government, because they were a people who were erased from the constitution as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, "national", where it appears there, means Serbs -- it could be "the Great Serb Assembly"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in that sense -- no, not in that sense of "people" in the sense of "nation". No, it would have said; "Great Serb Assembly". This is the citizens living on that territory, those people. The point was not to conduct a cleansing in this constitutional and legal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In no sense did I ask you that. You agree with me, though, that Serbs often refer to themselves as "nations", do you not -- you agree with that? There is nothing sinister in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but the Serbs cannot consider themselves to be a nation -- they are a nation, they are a people and I do not know what you consider yourselves to be, but we are a people, a nation, and we are an old nation, at that, and I consider this to be highly offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not aware of the fact that Mr. Fila was giving evidence in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with the Prosecutor. Besides, may I call your attention to article 1 of the exhibit we are discussing where mention is made of members of the "Serb nation" -- it is in article 1. You may proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, there were many --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, may I just say something? May I just say the following: I think that it is important -- the Serbs are a nation, and that is precisely what I wish to say, that here a distinction has to be made. I have to draw your attention to one of our special characteristics in this context, too. Serbs are a nation, yes, but until the present day in the constitution of the present Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, we call it "National Assembly", but we do not consider this Assembly to be the organ of Serbs. In this National Assembly there are representatives of other peoples, other nations, too, who live on the territory of the present day Serbia, and the representatives of national minorities, too, so I think it is a misunderstanding, really. I think I should interpret it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, in February 1991 -- in fact, on 21 February 1991, Croatia passed a law, which was entitled "the Constitutional Act Supplementing the Constitution Act of the Republic of Croatia". In that provision 9A, it says that: "In the Republic of Croatia, the provisions of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which are not in accord with the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, are repealed." It goes on to provide: "In the Republic of Croatia, the provisions of the Federal laws and other regulations and enactments of Federal agencies, which are not in accord with the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, and the laws of Croatia, are repealed." Is that a valid constitutional provision? Is that in accord with the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, since we had this discussion a few minutes ago, I did not hear the very beginning of what you said. Could you kindly repeat the beginning, so that I could give an accurate answer? We are talking about a particular act and a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means. On 21 February 1991, Croatia passed a law called "the Constitutional Act Supplementing the Constitution Act for the Implementation of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia" -- it is a large title, but that was the title of it. It provided, in part, in particular in article 9A that: "In the Republic of Croatia, the provisions of the Constitution of the SFRY, which are not in accord with the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, are repealed." It then goes on to say that enactments of Federal agency that were also not in accord with the Republic of Croatia's constitution, were also repealed. My simple question is: does that accord with the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean, were they declared unconstitutional, these provisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am asking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These provisions were in contravention to the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, that were both still in force at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Constitutional Court consider this law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Constitutional Court, the Federal Constitutional Court, did not consider this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that because it was legally valid and in accordance with the Constitution of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not because of that. Just one moment, please. I should like to remind you that the Constitutional Court, the Federal Constitutional Court, by its decision of 16 October, that is the relevant decision, 1991 -- it is the decision in which the judges participated, the judges of all the republics, and autonomous provinces -- it put a stop to the previous decision enacted on a sovereign and independent Republic of Croatia, and that decision to repeal implies an answer to this question. Everything that followed was considered unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you say that the decision of 16 October 1991, in fact, considered this law of Croatia of 21 February 1991 -- is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that it considered it, but it was binding, because the decisions of the Federal Constitutional Court are binding, final and executive and all acts which are along the same lines are considered unconstitutional. The constitutional decision on sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Croatia, on 25 June 1991, was, by the Federal Constitutional Court, ended, and there was no reason to go into other acts which were subordinate and relied upon that particular law. They had no foundations, because the constitution of the SFRY was reasserted, the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, by this act of the Federal Constitutional Court, was annulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are not seriously suggesting, are you, that this decision of the Constitutional Court was followed and applied in Croatia -- it was ignored, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is another question all together and not within my domain of expertise. For me, it is the decision which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you do not know whether it was followed or not -- is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think I need say whether I know whether it was applied or not. I do have knowledge on that matter and there was a whole series of events which were to follow and with the international community as an actor on the scene and organs within an internal level which were still functioning. Let me add the organs of the SFRY were functioning, and the Federal Assembly and the presidency of the SFRY, the Federal Constitutional Court was functioning and there is evidence to prove this, and that is what is important for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, either Croatia withdrew its declaration of independence, and went back to being a Republic of the SFRY in the true constitutional manner in accordance with this decision, or it embarked upon a programme of independence and sovereignty, did it not? It is very clear and everybody knows that Croatia became an independent State?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The Prosecutor knows that it became an independent State. I do not, so I do not think the witness should be asked more than what they wish to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, it did not become a State, an independent State. I adhere to the constitution, I respect constitutional norms and that is the supreme authority and supreme principle as an expert in constitutional law. What other people's conduct is, how they are going to behave, whether they are going to go against the constitution, that is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The whole issue here is whether or not Croatia became an independent State. You are asserting the act of independence was a nullity, and I cite for that this decision of the Constitutional Court. I am putting to you that the decision of the Constitutional Court was, at the end of the day, just totally ignored, was it not, except perhaps by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection. Mr. Niemann is not asking the question; he is presenting his views. I heard his views in the introduction and I shall hear it in his conclusion. The Professor is a witness and expert for constitutional matters -- not for the assertions of Mr. Niemann and the expert witness has explained the situation concerning the 1974 Constitution. If what happened was true, as Mr. Niemann states, then this would not be a topic for our expert here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I have the floor, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, may I ask you to rephrase your question as a question proper and relating to a legal issue without asserting your own views, but asking the witness to react on a legal matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the question, but might I say that I have stated a proposition which I would ask the expert to either agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I, Mr. President, your Honour -- (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked for the floor for a few minutes. May I just say one sentence, please, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be easier for us to proceed. I am fully conscious of the fact that Mr. Niemann has come here with questions which mean pre-supposed answers. However, it is my great desire and the reason for which I have come here is to clarify matters in the best possible way. The Faculty of Law in Belgrade delegated me as an expert in constitutional law to help us clarify matters and that is why I have looked upon everything with goodwill. I am not offended by the questions that demand set answers in the way that they were posed, but all these matters are contained in my expert report. I consider it to be unconstitutional, all acts which were enacted by the Republic of Croatia in that particular period, and I went even further, and I should like to remind you, one and all, that this is not just an unfounded attitude of ours that the Republic of Croatia was not an independent and sovereign republic at that time. I do not think I will go wrong if I remind you of an important fact within a series of many important facts that are linked to the international aspect, although that is not my job, but let me remind you that on 29 November 1991, the famous Badinter Commission considered Croatia's declaration of May 1991 by proclaiming its desire for independence. Therefore, I do not consider, and in that sense I should like to repeat, I do not consider that Croatia was an independent and sovereign republic and that is why, although this is not my duty -- I allowed myself to go beyond the frameworks of my particular task here -- but I think it would be a good idea if we were to adhere to the facts and, of course, to answer questions from my field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Professor. Let us confine ourselves to legal issues, but I would like to call upon you to address the legal issues, which are raised by the Prosecutor. I must say that it is clear to everybody that the Prosecutor is not asking questions waiting for pre-supposed answers, as you said. I think we are all looking for the truth and trying to understand what happened, and now, in this particular case, we are dealing with legal issues. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You had no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you now. Would you repeat what the President has said to me, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I was saying that we agree that we should now confine ourselves to legal issues and I would like to ask you whether you could also address the legal matters which are put to you and so let us proceed this way. Mr. Niemann, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, you were speaking of the fact that the Badinter Commission was an important authority when it comes to these issues -- you would agree with that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness might be shown exhibit 192, the Prosecution exhibit. (Handed). Professor, I am told that it is in the English language. Do you read the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like you to translate it for me for the purposes of exactitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, Professor. It is a little unfair of me to show you an English document, so, please, if you do not understand anything that I say, ask for clarification. Professor, this is an opinion of the Badinter Commission -- it is opinion number 11. I only want to go to one part of it, which is paragraph 4. I will read the English text of it and it can be translated to you. In paragraph 4 it says: "The issue is the same as regards the Republics of Croatia and Slovenia, both of which declared their independence on 25 June 1991 and suspended their declarations of independence for three months on 7 July 1991, as provided for by the Brioni Declaration. In accordance with the Declaration, the suspensions ceased to have effect on 8 October 1991. Only then did these two republics definitely break all links with the organs of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and become sovereign States in international law. For them, 8 October 1991 is the date of State succession." You would agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The facts that you have presented are exact, but that date -- by that date neither republics became sovereign and independent States. They were still members of the Federation of Yugoslavia, and they were not considered as independent States. I think that we shall have an opportunity of clarifying these matters through the next expert opinion, but we do not consider, and I do not consider, that they gained independence on that date, regardless of their desires and proclamations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you say Badinter is wrong -- at least in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I quoted the decision of the Badinter Commission dating back to 29 November 1991. This great act is proclaimed -- I say this conditionally -- the act of June, which was to come into force on the date that you mentioned, 8 October -- the commission considers it a desire for gaining independence and constituting independent and sovereign States. Therefore, there is no collision there, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Except that, where Badinter appears to agree with your position, you say that he is correct, but where he appears to differ from your position, you say that that is not correct; do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you put your question a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the Secretary-General of the United Nations, do you think he would be likely to get it right or wrong when it comes to a question of accepting the sovereignty of a State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not wish to give an answer, because I feel that it is outside the domain of my expertise, especially as I am -- and bearing in mind the fact that there is a separate expert's report, which will be the right occasion for us to discuss this matter. I have spoken about what I consider to be essential for this particular question, from the constitutional and legal aspects. I am not an expert in international public law, but I have placed this in the function of the constitutional and legal aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I do not want to press you in an area where you do not feel comfortable to comment. Going back, then, to the issue of the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the decision of Serbia on 2 July 1990 to hold a referendum on the question of Kosovo, was that in accordance with the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of 1974?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. First of all, I would like to see the decision and what referendum Mr. Niemann is talking about and what this has to do with Vukovar and the indictment that we are dealing with here. Kosovo is something that I am sure you will probably be discussing one day, but let Mr. Niemann show us the decision that he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, the question is quite relevant, because we are talking about issues of constitutional law. However, the witness is entitled to take a look at the relevant document. I wonder whether Mr. Niemann has the document so that the witness can -- or maybe the witness is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I ask my question in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware of this decision on the referendum? Are you aware, or do you need to take a look at the particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should first of all like to say that I do not think it is useful to expand our topic here. The subject is a very complex and important one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but this is for us to decide whether or not the question is relevant. Please, go on, but tell me whether you need a document, because then we could, after the break, if it is possible, provide you with the document so you can give your answer afterwards. Mr. Niemann, do you have the relevant document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know particularly what document it is. It is a referendum I am speaking of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: A decision on a referendum. Are you aware that there was a referendum in Serbia on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the referendum was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you ask again your question. I do not remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I will see if I can obtain any document on it, if necessary, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point is, Professor, that during --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, would you like to answer that question, or would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that we should not discuss that subject today. We do not have the relevant background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, that is up to us. Let us move on to another question, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point is, is it not, Professor, that during the period starting in late 1989 through to late 1991, there was a whole series of acts, which, whether they were technically in accordance with the SFRY Constitution or not, they certainly did not help it, that occurred in a number of the republics, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are discussing one republic here, yes, that is correct, but I think that, in that period, for me, something vital happened, when we are talking about legal facts -- something happened and there is evidence to bear this out. A series of acts followed, which meant an infringement of the unified constitutional system established by the existing Federal and Republican constitutions that were in force at the time and, in that sense, if I may just add, the Federal Constitutional Court did not only react towards what one or two republics did, but it reacted to everything which meant a violation of the constitution. I am mentioning the amendments which were enacted in 1989. All those amendments were under the scrutiny of the Federal Constitutional Court and it brought decisions on all these acts and all the republics were taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But notwithstanding the best efforts of the Constitutional Court, this process of disintegration continued at a pace, did it not, especially between 1989 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it did not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a complex question, which is considered in constitutional legal science. The causes of that situation are being studied and there will be a lot of time which will be needed to view the whole question in its entirety and to assess it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the process of disintegration of the federation was not something that just happened in Croatia; it happened in all of the republics in varying degrees, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The process of disintegration was characteristic for four republics, which are considered to be secessionist republics and which confirmed this by a series of legal and factual acts. They are Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, and Bosnia. What happened with Serbia and Montenegro is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting it was not in any way destructive of the federation, what happened in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you a simple answer to that question. My personal opinion is that Serbia tried, over a longer period of time and Montenegro as well, to retain Yugoslavia, both from the -- I say this both from the legal aspect and from the aspects of being a witness to the event, both in the legal realm and in actual fact. This question is related to history and I think that it will be interesting -- that is my recommendation -- to go back in time to history and take a look at history.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I think cited amongst the material is the decision on, I think, 23 July, when there was an order of the Parliament of Croatia to remove or dissolve the Assembly of Vukovar. I will just find the exhibit number so you can have a look at it. I think it is D5. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is alright.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have that one there? Do you consider that to be a valid and legally binding decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned that decision in my expert report and in connection with this concrete case, it is an order to undertake special measures in the municipality of Vukovar. It was enacted in 1991. The Municipal Assembly was dissolved, the Executive Council was relieved of its duties, and the mandate of the President of the Municipal Assembly ceased and that is what is essential for us here. At that particular moment, the deputy of the Government, representative of the Government of Croatia, was nominated, was appointed. All these were a series of events which, from the constitutional and legal aspect, did not coincide with the constitutional system of the SFRY and the Republic of Croatia, but they were separate circumstances and the whole thing -- that is how it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that it was not constitutional, so far as the SFRY was concerned. Do you say that it was legally valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not say that it is legally valid, but that it is a fact that that is how matters occurred, and everything evolved outside the constitutional norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, as a consequence of that, if the law was not legally valid, you would say that it has no effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not say that it did not have an effect. I am just looking at the legal dimension of the matter. Of course, it did have an effect and it was applied, that is a fact, but we are talking about non constitutional conduct under specific circumstances. This is something that the international community is well aware of -- it was involved in the situation there, not events that took place independently, and they are matters which were held under the control of the international community, and they reached agreements together for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, if it was not legally valid, then Mr. Dokmanovic continued on as the mayor of Vukovar or President of the Assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not continue being the mayor -- he could not, because the situation was such that this decree came into force and Mr. Marin Vidic, nicknamed Bili, was appointed the representative of the Croat Government, and by that act, the other person's functions ceased to exist on two counts. Mr. Dokmanovic ceased to perform that office. He could not act as President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are familiar with situations in history where the Royal family of this particular country we are in now had to go into exile during World War II -- nobody questioned in Holland the fact that they still remained the Royal Family of Holland, did they, and you know numerous instances of that in history, surely, in your readings you have seen that? The fact that one physically cannot perform the task is not the end of the matter, surely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not within the domain which I deal with, nor am I in a position to answer that question competently. Norm is one thing, and a factual situation is another thing. They may not coincide and that is a well known fact, but I am talking about legal aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I have shown you a law which you just said you do not consider to be legally valid. Now, I am putting to you that, if it is not legally valid, it has no effect. If it had no effect, Mr. Dokmanovic must have continued as the President of Vukovar, and I also put to you the fact that this is not something that has never happened before and, surely, you are not telling us that you do not know about situations like what happened in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you put your question in a more accurate way as a question relating to the particular situation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are not suggesting, are you, that -- Professor, are you signalling to Mr. Fila and he is signalling to you? I just saw you shake your head and look at him and he looked at you. You are not passing signals to each other by any chance, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I do not think so. Could you please try to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might say that this is the second time I have observed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Professor, could you dwell on this particular matter, namely, a legal act which is not constitutional under the Constitution of the Socialist Republic -- the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia -- whether this act, however effective, produced legal effects, was actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I have to point out that I am sorry if you have gained the impression that I am either giving signals to Mr. Fila, or receiving signals from him. I must tell you here that I am a representative of the Faculty of Law and I met Mr. Fila only when I was supposed to come here. We are involved in completely different matters, so spontaneously I look either at you or at him -- perhaps I am professionally used to addressing an audience, so you may rest assured on that account. I must say that the total situation we are dealing with here is unconstitutional, but it is not a question of law here. This is not a law, this is an order, this is a special situation. In this process of Croatia's separation, we have a sequence of acts that were passed in cooperation with the international community, I must say, in the common wish to get out of that crisis, but, from a formal point of view, or from a legal point of view, not even in the strictest sense but in any legal sense, all of these acts are not in line with the constitution, but what was happening was happening. Another office holder was appointed and he did function according to this order and that is a fact and it is another question altogether what things would have been like had everything been in keeping with legal and constitutional norms. All acts before and after this would have been dealt with in a constitutional manner, that is, in accordance with the constitution of the SFRY and this constitutional procedure is not an easy one, I must admit -- that is the only way in which it could be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mind if we take a recess now, probably for 20 minutes, so we now adjourn and we will reconvene at 10.30. (10.10 a.m.). (A short break). (10.30 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you said something -- I am sorry, we had already decided to have a recess --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, prior to the break, we were talking about the law of the Republic of Croatia -- or the order, I think you called it -- of Croatia on 23 July 1991 in relation to the municipality of Vukovar and its President and Deputy President. Was that law generally accepted by people of Serb nationality, who were living in the Vukovar municipality at the time, or who had left the Vukovar municipality -- was that a law that had been accepted by them, do you think, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about an order, not a law -- the difference is qualitative -- and it is important to differentiate between order and law, who brought in a law, or issued an order, and may I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, it is Exhibit D5. Professor, if you think that there is a distinction between "order" and "law" and that that is important, tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is precisely why I asked for the document, so that I can be precise. I have not got it. No -- I gave the document back. Yes, thank you, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have to stop for a moment -- we have a problem with the transcript. I think, professor, you wanted to tell us something about orders and laws before we go any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can make a distinction -- a "law" is a higher act than an "order" -- it is enacted by an assembly, whereas an order is an executive act by an organ of management and, as we see in the preamble, it is an order and it is enacted by the Minister of Justice -- a functionary at the head of the organ of management -- and he refers to the Croat law on administration and the Government of Croatia. It is a continuation of acts, whereas he refers to Article 130 of the Croat Constitution. An order is an act of implementation of a law and acts higher than an order. That is a category of individual acts, and it is one of a series of acts which came before organising power and authority. Here, the act is enacted by a Minister, and I do not know from the constitutional and legal aspect whether I can say that the Serb people supported the act or not -- in the true sense of the word, we cannot say that, whether it was generally accepted or not. It was a specific situation. We know that it was a specific situation and in the whole entire situation there were many acts which go beyond a legal order and legal system. This is an act which was applied and was followed by another concrete act, which was implemented, and which dissolved the particular person, Mr. Dokmanovic -- I said this yesterday -- he was relieved of his duties by the Serb authorities of the function of President of the municipal assembly. I think that is the key question that we wish to reach here, so his function ceased on both counts, according to the decision of the Croat authorities and the Serb authorities, that is to say, the authorities of the territory under the control of the Serb authorities. Let me say once again that we are dealing with a provisional organisation of power and authority under specific conditions -- in the process of disintegration, on the one hand and, on the other hand, ways and means were sought in Croatia as they were in other republics to do this in the best possible way -- in the most painless possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said you do not know whether or not it was accepted or not, but this was a decision of 24 July 1991. The law that I showed you of the Serb district of exhibit 16A -- that is a law of 25 September 1991 and it provides in Article 3, does it not, that "all State authorities, local government authorities, and other bodies and organisations of the Republic of Croatia (Handed) shall cease functioning in the area of the Serb district" -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The effect of that then is that, if this is a valid law, then if the law of 24 July, or the order of 24 July, even if it was valid, the effect of this law is that, whatever may have transpired as a consequence of the 24 July order, this overrides it, does it -- if that is not clear, please ask me and I will try and clarify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have here an order which we discussed a moment ago, and we have a law -- a constitutional law governing the territory under Serb control. These acts were enacted in the same process and their legal situation is the same -- or very similar. Article 3 of the law you mentioned -- it is the constitutional law for the Serb district dated the 25th (INAUDIBLE) of 1991, states that all State organs will cease to function as well as the organs of local self-government, and I should like to emphasise that provisional organs are set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point I make, professor, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you can answer it perhaps with a "Yes" or "No" answer, it will be a lot quicker, otherwise we will be here for a very long time, if we have detailed explanations to every question I put, so if you can possibly answer "Yes" or "No", I think it would speed up the process a great deal. The point I put to you, though, is this, is it not: you say that the Croat law, which had the effect of dismissing Mr. Dokmanovic and introducing a new regime, was an invalid law or an invalid order -- I think you said that in your evidence. Then I asked you whether or not it was a law that was accepted by the Serb people and you said to that that you did not know for sure, but then I point you to Article 3, and I say to you, does that not suggest to you that the Serb people, from the Vukovar area, did not accept the Croat law, but introduced their own law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not accepted. I think that the situation is clear. We are talking about two territories -- one under the control of Croatia and the other under the control of somebody else. I cannot say "Yes" or "No", because I might go wrong, but both sides established a provisional authority according to which power and authority is taken over by other organs until the situation is clarified and the law states "until the situation is resolved".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, as a strict constitutionalist, you would have to agree with me, would you not, that both of the laws do not comply with the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's 1974 Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They do not comply, like all the previous Acts which led to secession, and all the ones that came to follow, but they were accepted and came into force and were respected and implemented. As I say, it was a specific situation. The provisional territorial organisation of power and authority -- if you would have a broader interpretation of these particular documents, they were Acts which should be considered valid within the whole context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Under the 1974 Constitution, each of the republics and the autonomous provinces was given a prominent role in Government by having a seat on the Federal presidency; that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only in the presidency but in all the key organs of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was to avoid the concentration of power in the hands of one person, or in one group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and an equal participation of all the factors of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the purpose of this was so that power was distributed so that it would be Government by a consensus, with each of the republics expressing its interest -- there was an understanding that at the end, the decision would be taken by the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a constitutional provision -- all the organs of the federation set up on a parity basis and representation by the republics and provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This system was dependent on each of the republics and autonomous provinces coming to the presidency free to represent its own people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it envisaged, then, that one man should come to control the votes of the representatives of the four republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which man you have in mind -- the presiding individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am just talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or during Josip Broz Tito's lifetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was talking about the constitution itself in general terms and it is a general legal question and does not have to be related to specific events as such. I am just saying that the whole object of the constitution was to avoid a situation whereby one person would get a majority of the votes, whether it be of the republics or of the autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are generally correct, but let us say more precise terms -- a collective organ is collectively decided, everybody is equal in the decision making process, there is one presiding individual which is rotated and has no extra rights than everybody else in that particular body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, you would agree with me, I think, that it would be contrary to the constitution for the autonomy of provinces such as Kosovo and Vojvodina to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Removed from?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Removed from those provinces -- they have autonomy, and a voice under the 1974 Constitution. If that autonomy and voice is taken away, that would be contrary to the constitution, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The autonomy that we had in 1984, I am prepared to say this, was not an autonomy, a real autonomy. The autonomy of -- the autonomous provinces by the constitution gained a status which meant the status of a State, which does not exist anywhere and that was within the frameworks of one republic, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, the point I am trying to make is that under the constitution, it was envisaged that they would have autonomy and a voice in the sense that they had a vote on the presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether by constitution they could have a vote and voice -- that is to say, whether in 1989 the status of autonomy -- of the autonomous provinces could be altered in that respect, the status that they enjoyed previously according to the previous constitution, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Previous to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it was constitutional to change these factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am talking about the 1974 Constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Constitution of the Republic of Serbia dating back to 1974 and 1989 was the year when this was changed. The status was changed in 1989, and the autonomous provinces were given back the status that corresponded to the status of autonomy in the theoretical sense and in the international model sense, but this was done on the basis of a constitutionality through amendments to the constitution. It was not done unconstitutionally and it was done along with the participation of the representatives of the autonomous provinces in the legal organs that enacted those amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about blocking the rotation of the presidency, so when the representative of one republic's turn came up to become President of the presidency, is that something which is in accordance with the letter and spirit of the 1974 Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in accordance with rotation for a one year term.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, if you stopped that from happening, if you prevent that from happening, that is not in accordance with the letter and spirit of the 1974 Constitution, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if this is done democratically, by legally elected organs and according to constitutional procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, there was a constitutional amendment, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might assist us, Professor, by taking us to the constitutional amendment of 1989, or telling us about it, which permitted the rotation of the presidency to not occur -- for that to be blocked by political means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not blocked -- it was a change in another sense -- a broader sense. It was not a change of organisation that had taken place; it was a change in the status of the provinces within the frameworks of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
