utterances.text: Your Honours, we are talking about two constitutions here. There seems to be a misunderstanding. The 1989 amendment has to do with the constitution of Serbia and, when Mr. Niemann is talking about a constitution, could he please tell us which constitution he has in mind, because we are now talking about Serbia's constitution altering the position of Kosovo, not the Federal constitution by which the presidency is rotated with Mr. Mesic, so would Mr. Niemann please tell us what constitution he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it to be that the rotation held true until the constitution was valid and that we are talking about changes in the Republic of Serbia and that is why I reacted to the question about rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, no, I may have been confusing there. What I was talking about was certainly Kosovo and Vojvodina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel that there seems to be a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is. I was talking about it initially and then I moved on. What I moved on to was the rotation of the President of the Federal presidency, when Stipe Mesic was prevented from taking his seat on 15 May 1991. I put it to you that that was not a decision which was either in accordance with the letter or spirit of the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One is the spirit of the constitution, rotation was not changed and Stipe Mesic was the legal and legitimate President of the presidency until 5 December 1991 the presidency for which the authentic principle held true, the principle of rotation, determined by the Federal constitution. So the misunderstanding is only in that we were talking about two levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had in mind the changes which took place, whereas you had in mind rotation, but I think we understand each other now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you are not suggesting, are you, that when Stipe Mesic was due to take up his position of President of the presidency on 15 May 1991 and that was blocked and that it was only through the intervention of the international community that the process was deblocked, if I may use that term, to allow him to take up his position -- you are not suggesting that that did not happen, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I maintain that it was his turn. The way in which he took over his appointment, I do not think I need go into here and now, but the essential thing is that he did take over this function and performed this function until the date I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the statement by Slobodan Milosevic on 16 March 1991, when he said that "Yugoslavia had entered into its final phase of agony" and that the "Republic of Serbia will no longer recognise a single decision reached by the presidency under existing circumstances, because it would be illegal" -- would you agree with me that that was hardly something that could be said to be in accordance with the letter or spirit of the 1974 Constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, when Mr. Niemann is speaking about a document, could he please read the document and could we have a look at it? Are we talking about evidence offered by the Prosecution? I have not seen this exhibit. Could he please read this to us, the authentic text, and then I shall agree to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One more thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, have you got --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was in the evidence of the witness Mesic when he came here and testified, your Honours. I do not have the reference at the moment, I can find out. It is a simple proposition. If the witness does not know anything about it, then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you know about this declaration by Mr. Milosevic on 16 March 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about it. I would have to have a look at the document itself, but I wish to say that many statements were made by responsible persons, not only Slobodan Milosevic, I could quote others, too, but I do not really want to do so. I do not think that we should be discussing that here. I do not think it is relevant. There were different statements that were made at the time and I would never agree to them and I am just mentioning this in passing, but I do not want to go into political statements now, because if they are evidence, we should have them here and compare them to other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I am asking you to either agree or disagree. It is a very simple thing. If you do not know anything about it, you can say, "I do not know anything about it", that is fine. Surely it is easy enough for you to say whether you agree that that is in accordance with the spirit and letter of the constitution -- you are supposed to be an expert in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I would have to have a look at the text, so that I could present my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the same day, the Serbs of Knin declared their independence from Croatia, that is the very same day as Slobodan Milosevic made this statement, do you think the Serbs of Knin declaring their independence from Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, again, we have not said in a relevant fashion that Milosevic ever made this kind of statement and who is this Milosevic in this period in 1991? Secondly, we also have not established when this Knin proclaimed its independence and it is not true they proclaimed their independence but it is not up for me to say so. But, if Prosecutor Niemann is saying that someone proclaimed something, then show the proclamation. We cannot make allegations of this kind or can we say something in relation to something which may, to put it politely, exist in the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot present my position on something that I am not aware of -- that I am not aware of in a reliable fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you do not know of this proclamation of independence by the Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it is not even true, but I cannot really say this, because I would have to have the text in front of me. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Alright. Can we move on to questions with regard to which you have documents, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I need to respond to what Mr. Fila is putting up. It is not necessary for me to produce documents to everything I am saying. If the witness does not know anything about it, the witness can say, "I do not know about that" and we can move on. I do not have to go through a process of tendering a whole lot of material. This witness comes to us an expert. One would have thought that every detail and matter that occurs in relation to the Constitution of 1974 would be something that she is familiar with. If she is not, we will move on to the next matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Alright.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, I have to intervene once again. The witness is an expert in constitutional law and, for that which exists -- not for that which does not exist -- and it is not true at all that Knin had proclaimed its independence in 1991 -- perhaps this exists somewhere in the Office of the Prosecutor in somebody's thoughts. We are not talking about experts for something that does not exist. No-one is an expert in that which does not exist. No-one is an expert in fantasy. Also, it is offensive to say that the expert is supposed to know about something which does not exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I protest for linking my expertise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Fila, the expert witness is an expert on constitutional law, and I assume she knows everything about constitutional law in the Republic of Yugoslavia and the former Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As well as, possibly, she may know about the historical events which have some relevance, from the viewpoint of constitutional law. If she has no knowledge of particular events which have a dimension relevant to the constitutional law, she may simply say, "I do not know. I am not familiar with those events" and we move on to other questions. May you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We absolutely understand each other. If questions are put the way they are put everywhere in the world, did Knin proclaim its independence and when, and Mr. Niemann is saying that Knin had proclaimed its independence -- that is not a question, that is a claim and it is a claim which is untrue, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will deal with this in our rebuttal case, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, we were talking about these autonomous provinces. I do not want to ask you about events that specifically happened necessarily, but I do want to get to the bottom of this question of changing the status of the autonomous provinces. Is it your evidence that this is a matter entirely for the particular Republic of Serbia in relation to Kosovo and Vojvodina, that it has nothing to do with the Federal Government, or the Federal Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is related. The autonomous provinces are part of one republic, the Republic of Serbia, and according to the constitution of 1974, they were also a constituent element of the federation, but the position of the autonomous provinces was essentially regulated by the constitution of Serbia, and then certain changes were introduced by way of amendments to the constitution of Serbia, and this was done by the authorities on which the representatives of the autonomous provinces themselves had seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Among the documents that you included in support of your paper -- and I believe this is one that you rely upon as opposed to the next expert -- was a copy of the official Gazette of the Municipality of Vukovar of 28 March 1990, which dealt with amendments to the Statute of the municipality. Do you remember that document? If you want the document, please ask for it, and it can be made available to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I have the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was an amendment to the Statute, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please, could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is your document, professor. I am not sure it has been admitted. I assume --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not got it with me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Fila has it there then?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have not admitted this into evidence -- the Statute of the municipality -- so I do not really know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am talking about the amendment on 28 March.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This was not submitted into evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is it D4?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let me try and approach it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is an amendment to the Statute of the Municipality of Vukovar and I am just interested in Article 202(a). Firstly, I think I should establish -- is this a document that you relied upon when you prepared your report? I am not asking Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not something you relied on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Have you got a copy of this document, Mr. Niemann, in Serb?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, in Serb. I have a Serb version of it -- it is not easy to read. Perhaps it might be shown to Mr. Fila and then the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sure I have it, but it is at the hotel, because I do not have everything here with me. You know how many documents I have -- my room is full and I really do not know what Mr. Niemann is going to bring up in his questioning. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand this document was produced by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, as supporting material and I do not object to Mr. Niemann tendering this into evidence at all, if he wishes so, but what I propose for expertise is what I presented as evidence, so this was not really given to the witness to have a look at it, but I am not opposed to it at all, because Mr. Niemann is finally putting questions that are based on documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want to ask any questions about it if the witness did not rely upon it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I based my expert opinion on the Statute of the Municipality of Vukovar, I also have that document. I also have it in the hotel. I have it with me, because I always take all my relevant papers with me. This photocopy is -- let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, I understand there is a problem with the transcript. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, is this a document you are familiar with and did you rely on it in any way when you prepared your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I drew on the Statute and I had this document as well, but I do not know in what context I could fit it into my expert opinion, and what is it specifically about, Sir. When we are talking about the changes to the Statute -- I mean Article 202(a).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to know what "nations" and "nationalities" meant -- whether you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This expression of ours "nations" and "nationalities", this is a special term that we used and we had replaced "nationalities" -- we had replaced the term "national minorities" by "nationalities" in the former Yugoslavia. In the world, people call it "national minorities", but our authors of the constitution wanted to qualify them as "nationalities".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have no further questions. As far as I am concerned, the witness can be released, but before the next witness is brought in, I kindly request that we see the next video clip that I obtained -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be convenient to exhibit this document, since we have referred to it -- the Official Gazette, 28 March 1990 -- it might be convenient to give it the next D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless you have any objection, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, if you do not mind, I would like to ask you a few questions. First of all, would you agree with the proposition made by Defence counsel in his opening statement, and I read out from the written text: "That the accused Slavko Dokmanovic was a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Republic of Croatia, as were the victims who tragically perished." Would you agree, therefore, that Mr. Dokmanovic had, in November 1991, a dual nationality -- he was simultaneously a national of the Federal State as well as a national of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Then how would you legally explain the purport and meaning of Article 4 of a law which we have been discussing this morning -- the law concerning the implementation of the constitutional law passed on 25 November 1991 by the Great National Assembly of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Article 4 states of this law -- and you probably have it in front of you -- which we have already mentioned this morning provides and I quote: "On the date on which the constitutional law takes effect, all the inhabitants of the Serb District shall cease to be citizens of the Republic of Croatia, retaining their citizenship of Yugoslavia." So, in a way, if I understand this provision correctly, that means that, according to this law passed by the Great National Assembly of the Serb District and so on, those people who were Croat citizens and lived in the area of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem ceased to be regarded as citizens of the Republic of Croatia. I just want to ask you to clarify, from a legal point of view, this situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, the constitution of the SFRY is valid, as far as SFRY citizenship is concerned, and the Federal law on citizenship, which regulates this particular matter and the rest of your quotation is something that we have already had an opportunity to discuss. These were circumstances that I tried to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, that means, if I understand you correctly, that according to you, this provision, Article 4 of the law which I just mentioned, is inconsistent or contrary to the relevant Federal laws of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, because they, in a way, decide that the citizens of Republic of Croatia, living in a particular area, cease to retain their nationality, and only retain the citizenship of Yugoslavia, so therefore this particular provision is in conflict with the Federal law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like many Acts before that and after that, if we were to subject them to constitutional and legal expertise under normal conditions, I do not really think it is relevant in relation to everything that we spoke of in this context and from the point of view of this particular case. I think that the introductory statement is alright, as far as this point is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Professor, I am asking you a legal question and, if you do not mind, it is for the court to decide whether an issue is relevant or is not relevant to our particular case. Please, therefore, answer my question, if you are in a position to answer this question, from a purely legal viewpoint. We are not dealing with facts; we are dealing with legal issues. As I say, I think I understood you to say that this -- I may be wrong -- particular provision was not consistent with the Federal law of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. If I am wrong, you can tell me that I understood you incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitution and the Federal law of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have to stop for a few minutes, because we cannot get the transcript. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will proceed. I want to understand, what nationality people living in the area of Vukovar between September and November 1991 possessed -- people who were born there, who had been for the whole of their life citizens of the Republic of Croatia, and by the same token, at the same time, also of course citizens of the Federal State, at that point in time, between September and, say, November or December 1991, whether they still possessed this dual nationality -- the nationality of the Republic of Croatia, plus the nationality of the Federal State -- it is a very simple legal question, regardless of the particular position of the accused. As I say, let us say, people of Serb ethnic origin living in Vukovar or in the area of Vukovar, who had been there for many years, who were born there, were they still in this particular period nationals -- sorry, let us say citizens of both the Republic of Croatia and of the Federal State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you do not mind, I would like to ask you another question. We have been provided a document -- a law on Croat citizenship passed in Croatia on 26 June 1991 and this is Prosecution exhibit 190A and I wonder whether the Registrar could be so kind as to provide the witness with a copy in Serbo-Croat. I wonder whether you are familiar with this law -- the law on Croat citizenship passed on 26 June 1991 -- only the English version? Sorry, professor, I apologise, I understand now from the Registrar that we have not been given the original Serbo-Croat text, so I will therefore skip this question, but you may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we do have it. Mr. Niemann gave us the Serb version, too -- I mean, the Croat version. Perhaps he did not, I do not know. The Prosecutor promised us a copy, but I do not know whether we actually received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is the law on Croat citizenship of 26 June 1991, Prosecution exhibit 190A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We gave it yesterday to Ms. Lopicic, I understand -- that is what I am instructed, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You gave us the Constitution -- the Constitution of Croatia, not the law on citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Professor, if you do not mind, I will read out a few provisions -- these are long texts, but I will read out only a few provisions. This law amends previous laws on the citizenship of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. Can you follow me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As a lawyer, reading this particular law, I got the impression that it was not drafted as a law on citizenship of a republic of the Federal State, but, rather, as the law of a sovereign State. For instance -- because it covers so many issues which are normally covered by the legislation on nationality on any sovereign country -- France, Italy, Germany and so on. For instance, at the end, it states in Article 28: "The certificate of citizenship is a public document which serves to prove Croat citizenship and is issued by the Municipal Registrar's Office, or" -- and I underline this part -- "the authorised diplomatic or Consular Office of the Republic of Croatia abroad." So, therefore, it implies that it is dealing with the citizenship, not as the citizenship which, in a way, supplements the Federal citizenship of the Federal State but, rather, as a citizenship of a sovereign country. So this is the impression which one gets from reading this law, and afterwards in Article 29 it is stated: "Croat citizenship is evidenced by a valid identity card, military identity card or passport." So, assuming that I am right, but I might be wrong -- I would like to have your view -- assuming that this is therefore conceived of as this sort of typical nationality or citizenship law of a sovereign country, would this law be inconsistent with the federal legislation of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, because it starts out from the fact that the Republic of Croatia is a sovereign independent State and that, as such, it could regulate the citizenship of a sovereign State. However, as Croatia at that time was still not a sovereign and independent State, then it follows that this law is not in conformity either with the constitution of federal Yugoslavia and the federal laws governing the citizenship of the SFRY, nor is it in harmony with the previous law of the Socialist Republic of Croatia as a member of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, I take your point, but, in a way, would I be right in also inferring from your reply that, mutatis mutandis, this would also apply to the law which we were discussing previously passed on 25 September 1991 by the Great National Assembly of the Serb Districts of Slavonia. To the extent, this law also provided for regulated matters of citizenship and therefore could not be regarded probably as consistent with the federal law on citizenship -- I think that probably I was a bit convoluted. I do not know whether my question is clear. If it is not clear, I could put it in a better way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please, would you put it in a clearer way, although I do follow your trend of thought?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was meaning that I see some parallelism between the enactment -- the passing by the Republic of Croatia of a law on citizenship, and the passing by the Great National Assembly of the Serb District of Slavonia of a law which includes a provision of citizenship. Could we say that, also, this Article 4 of that particular law of Slavonia and so on is not consistent with the federal constitution or the federal laws on citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not draw a comparison here, in the context of everything that we have said beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: My final question relates to the legal nature of this entity, which we have been mentioning so many times, but which we are not very clear, at least the court is not very clear about -- this Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem which had a Government, President and assembly and so on, could you please clarify the legal status of this District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, the fact that it had a Government, assembly and a President, was it a government, a regional entity? From the viewpoint of the federal constitution, what was the legal status of this entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was specific, to say the least, and I could not incorporate it into the ruling federal constitution, but it can be fitted into the circumstances that both Croatia, Yugoslavia and this particular district found itself in and the fact that it was a question of a provisional situation -- temporary situation -- which was qualified as such until the final solution to the problem was reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the setting up of the government of the autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja and so on, was not fully in keeping or in conformity or in accordance with the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a question of provisional organs and, strictly speaking, it was not in keeping with the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it a sort of -- it is called "government of the district". Was it a sort of de facto local government, was it a body, was it a region? Judging from your experience as an expert in constitutional law, how would you classify or characterise the nature of this body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the constitutional legal aspects, I cannot incorporate it into any classical model, I must tell you, because there are models of the organisation of a State regardless of whether it is a unitarian state or a federal state -- internal organisation. We are talking about the temporary constitution of a district which is under the control of the Serbs, and it is being organised provisionally in order that daily life may function, and in order that the questions vital to the population can be regulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Alright. As you know in international law, we have an expression which is also used by constitutional lawyers "de facto government", so a sort of provisional entity, which is set up due to historical circumstances and which normally therefore disappears for various reasons. Leaving aside this possible classification as de facto government, could you explain to us, again strictly from a legal viewpoint, the relations between this Government of the autonomous district of Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem and the central authorities in Belgrade -- the federal authorities, one; and, two, the central authorities of the Republic of Serbia, because I understand this was in the area within the territory of the Republic of Serbia. I may be wrong, but -- the legal relationships?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The legal relationship does not exist here. It is a question of the territory of the Republic of Croatia with the Serb population as the constituent titular nation, which hold a given territory under their control and, in the legal aspects, we cannot speak of a relationship with the authorities in the matrix State -- a State which is a matrix State for that particular nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This again clarifies -- I apologise for my ignorance. I thought that Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem would also cover part of the territory of the Republic of Serbia proper -- not only Eastern Slavonia but also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness shakes head).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. Therefore, this region --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is where the misunderstanding lies -- it is the Republic of Croatia and the territory of Croatia, where the majority population is Serb, not as of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there are any questions relating to the issues which I have asked? There is no objection to the witness being released? Professor, thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I suggest that now we take a look at the videotape you mentioned before and then we break at quarter to 12 until 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before this videotape is played, let me give you some explanations -- it is the tape from a cassette given by the Prosecutor. It is Mr. Dokmanovic's appearance in 1993, two years after the events which are relevant to the case, but I should like to draw your attention to the following fact: I should like to draw your attention to the fact that count 19 of the indictment, which states that Slavko Dokmanovic, in November 1991, after the fall of Vukovar, took over once again the function of the President of the Municipal Assembly and continued that function until mid 1996, so the Prosecutor states that Mr. Dokmanovic, until, if I understand correctly, he was arrested, he was President and he probably is still. That is why 1993 is an important date. Please pay attention to the signature underneath -- may the signature be translated, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "A life of dignity, existence". (Videotape played). "The people of Vukovar explain why so little has been done to rebuild Vukovar. It is the consequence of military engagement because the most capable are on the front-line, because rifles are still the most important thing. Vukovar is the largest town in the Republic of Serbia and Krajina. It is a symbol of the struggle as was never seen in these areas. Probably it is the result of the mixture of the population that exists in these parts and, in view of everything that Vukovar suffered and what the people of Vukovar gave for the Republic of Serbia and Krajina, we expect that, with its rebirth and its reconstruction, we symbolise the rebirth and creation of the State of Serbia and Krajina, as we expect it to be, as it will no doubt be. Therefore, I do not think we will --"

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like a translation of the signature under the photograph -- that is the key question -- the caption under the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It says "Slavko Dokmanovic, former mayor of Vukovar". That is the caption.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it states in the text "two years later" -- "two years after that". I would like this to be admitted as evidence by the Prosecutor, because it is the Prosecutor's tape, and I think that this would be a good moment to propose to the court that, as evidence of the Defence in connection with this caption, because they are all from Radio Television Serbia, that the following documents be admitted, so that we can see who wrote the captions, both from the Prosecutor's aspect and the aspects of the Defence. There are other things that are not very convenient either to me or the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The amendment to the Statute will be D23 and the English translation D23A, although I do not have an English translation yet. I do not know whether the Prosecution can provide the Registry with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is the Registry page D6688.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will be able to find it. I am not really certain about the video, whether the Defence would like to have it admitted as a Defence or Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like it to be the Prosecutor's exhibit, because it is the Prosecution's tape. It is the same tape where we saw the first two segments played to us by the Prosecution and this is the third segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I certainly have no objection to it being tendered as our exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution exhibit 193.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I have just given you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might we see this document, your Honours? I do not think we have seen it -- we may have, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me explain. It is a confirmation from Radio Television that the caption seen on the videotape, which we call krijons, are made in the television building itself, and not on the spot -- on location; the caption was made in the television building by television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, it is the date -- I thought you said the video was 1993. The reference here is to a news programme of 21 November 1991 -- this is in the document that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This document refers to the first tape -- the first Prosecution evidence, where it states "the mayor", but I accept that the part of "1993" which suits my purpose was also written on the premises of the television. I accept what the Prosecutor uses is correct. So, I do accept that document to my own debit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our objection originally to the admission of this document was the fact that, in this footage from 21 November, it is not just a reference that is put in there in a vacuum. In fact, the reporter says, "I am here with Slavko Dokmanovic, the mayor of Vukovar" and then he turns to him and asks a question. This, in and of itself, seems to imply this was put on by someone in Belgrade without any information whatsoever. That was the reason we objected to it. We would still maintain that objection because of this date and that there is no reference to the date for 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think you know that I never use tricks -- perhaps somebody else uses tricks to prove a point. I gave you the document only for what is written and what Mr. Williamson says, that the reporter is speaking and says, "This is the mayor of Vukovar", I have no objection there whatsoever. He really does say that. What Mr. Williamson says is quite correct. The document refers to the caption alone, so we are talking about two different matters here. I do not question the exactitude of what Mr. Williamson is saying. It was something that the journalist in question stated, but the captions, with this segment of the footage and with the other tape dating back to 1993, were done in the television offices -- that is the sense of the document. I do not see where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If that is Mr. Fila's position now, we would have no objection, but if I do recall correctly, he did raise an objection to this film being admitted originally and it was overruled by the court. So, I just wanted to make this absolutely clear, that this was not an effort to get around that in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is admitted. This letter will be D24.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, and the English translation D24A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will now adjourn for 15 minutes until 5 past 12. (11.49 a.m.). (12.08 p.m.).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we get to the witness, I just had one brief matter to clear up. In relation to this videotape which has been entered as exhibit 193, it is necessary for us to copy it on to an additional tape, which we will submit later to the Registry, we have arranged this. I just wanted to point out in response to Mr. Fila's statements in connection with the videotape, we had already entered into an agreement with the Defence -- a stipulation to the effect that Slavko Dokmanovic was not the mayor in 1993, and that he was re-elected as President of the Vukovar assembly on 10 June 1994. This was communicated to the Defence on 25 March. This is not an issue that we are contesting. IVAN CUKALOVIC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Examination-in-chief by MR. FILA:

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you feel comfortable, Mr. Cukalovic, can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I feel comfortable, but it is not altogether pleasant, like in any court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have a degree in law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you get a MA in 1982 at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you get your Ph.D. in 1985, also in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you now a full Professor of International Public Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an Associate Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During your career, did you take courses in Moscow, London, The Hague and elsewhere in international public law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this document -- this is your curriculum vitae and say if it is correct, and did you write all these articles and books that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked as D25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is the CV (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, could we show the expert the next document, too, five copies in the Serb language and five copies in the English language. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D26, and the English translation D26A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D27 and D27A. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have the impression that Mr. Niemann wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not rise to object to the admission of these documents or particularly the report, but I wish to make the following observation: this is an International Tribunal and I presume that this witness will now opine on international law and on conclusions which ultimately your Honours will need to decide upon and I will, at the end of the day, be arguing that whatever testimony you receive from this witness should be given no greater weight than what would be submitted from the bar table by the Prosecution side, having regard to the fact that he is touching upon matters which are within the expertise of the court and is to be distinguished, for example, from the last witness, who was giving expert testimony on matters of foreign law -- domestic law, if your Honours please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I wonder whether we could try to restrict ourselves to legal issues relevant to the present case, generally speaking -- legal issues of public international law relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my brief, I said how many hours I need for my expert opinions and I am going to have that time. I am going to cut it by a half, but you see how long the cross-examination takes, so it does not really depend on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you the author of the articles and books presented in this CV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay, I already asked you that. Is this your expert opinion and is it also an amendment to your expert opinion? I wish this to be admitted into evidence, please. If I am not mistaken, there are no objections from the other side. The Defence fully agrees with the question that you have put, and the Defence has one question only for this witness. I really cannot be any shorter than that. What is the nature of the armed conflict that happened on the territory of Croatia within the SFRY in the period which is important for this indictment -- which is relevant to this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to draw conclusions on this crucial matter, certain questions have to be answered before that, which cast more light on the nature of the war on the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was a special war from many points of view. Also, in view of the fact that on the same territory, during the past 50 years, two conflicts were waged between the same protagonists and with tragic consequences, as we can see. The first conflict between ethnic groups on the territory of the former Yugoslavia occurred parallel to the German occupation, which led to the disintegration of the then Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the establishment of the independent State of Croatia, Greater Albania, Bulgaria, on the territory of the disintegrated Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The second conflict broke out 50 years later -- its objective was to change territorial sovereignty and to create independent ethnic states. In order to draw a conclusion as to the nature of the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we are going to start with a gradual analysis, because only this comparative historical legal method can give arguments to this court, so that it can conclude whether the conflict on the territory of the former SFRY was an international or internal conflict. The period after the first disintegration of Yugoslavia, the first break-up of Yugoslavia after 1941, is marked by problems that were resolved only superficially. In 1918, the first Yugoslavia was established -- there were three constituent peoples, Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and only Serbs brought into Yugoslavia their independent statehood together with Montenegro, of course. In the second Yugoslavia in 1945 onwards, divisions only grew through quasi constitutional mechanisms. The number of constituent peoples was increased from three to six, and every one of these peoples had their own republic. It should be noted that the composition of the population of each republic was mixed from an ethnic point of view. In 1968, in Croatia, the so-called Maspok, the mass political movement, occurred in Croatia and it homogenised the Croat people. Belgrade Press was burned down and cars with Serb registration plates were demolished and army personnel were attacked, et cetera. The crisis was over. The leadership resigned and proceedings were instituted before a court of law against Franjo Tudjman, President of the Republic of Croatia, because of hostile activities. In the 1970s, Yugoslavia faced its first terrorist groups, which came into the Yugoslav territory in 1972 and these were Croat terrorists. Soon afterwards, in 1980, Josip Broz Tito died. He was a person who, in a way, kept Yugoslavia together as a single State and then political Parties were first established. The problem was that, in each and every republic, a national Party came into power, and their objective was separation. With the exception of some republics, like Serbia and Montenegro, the political leadership that won the elections in Serbia and Montenegro were in favour of maintaining Yugoslavia. In order to find a way out of this difficult situation, the members of the presidency visited the republican centres trying to reach a solution how Yugoslavia could be preserved. However, Croatia started importing weapons illegally. Martin Spegelj, the former Minister of Defence of Croatia, said that secret arms purchases were made from Switzerland with the assistance of Hungary -- I quote -- "for the needs of the Croat army that was secretly being organised", so at that time already paramilitary units were secretly being formed in Croatia. In the expose of the presidency of the SFRY on 17 October 1990, the following is said: "Relations between individual Federal units have deteriorated to such an extent that contacts at the level of responsible organs have been cut off altogether or have been reduced to confrontation -- even armed threats are being made." In 1990, the Ministry of Defence of Yugoslavia documented the illegal import of weapons into Slovenia and Croatia, and the presidency of Yugoslavia on 9 January 1991 passed an order on the disbandonment of all paramilitary formations and in response to that Croatia said the following: "The Republic of Croatia, in Defence of its economic and political sovereignty, shall use all means available and shall mobilise the entire Croat people at home and abroad, world-wide." Stipe Mesic, at that time the President of Yugoslavia, said the following: "Croatia has opted for Defence and has armed itself." Soon, there was an escalation of a conflict between Croat paramilitary units and Serbs on the territory of Croatia who had self organised their people, because they had learned an historical lesson from the experience of the Second World War, which you had an opportunity to see yesterday, on the videotapes. On this occasion, another statement was made and that is that this was nothing but the beginning of a new civil war. At the meeting of the presidency of Yugoslavia and the supreme command of Yugoslavia, it was proposed to introduce a state of emergency in order to stop a civil war and to reach agreement on how relations in the country should be regulated. However, the majority of votes was against this proposal. Soon after that, Croatia launched a diplomatic offensive and paid visits to members of the European Union, Rome, Moscow, et cetera. On 1 June 1991, Stipe Mesic was elected President of Yugoslavia. Only two days after that, he asked Germany for the recognition of Slovenia and Croatia and I quote the former German Ambassador to Yugoslavia, Horst Graber: "Most are dishonourable, they do not speak the truth. They conceal their true intentions in their attempt to instrumentalise and abuse the international community." On 25 June 1991, on the basis of the vote of their citizens beforehand, they passed a charter of independence, of the Republic of Slovenia and on the same day, Croatia adopted a constitutional decision on sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Croatia. How did the Federal authorities react to this? As regards these decisions to leave Yugoslavia, the Constitutional Court annulled articles 2, 3 and 4 of the declaration proclaiming independence of Slovenia and also the declaration proclaiming the Sovereign and Independent Republic of Croatia and they ruled as follows: "The right of the peoples to self-determination, including the right to secession laid down by the SFRY constitution may not, in the opinion of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, be exercised by the unilateral enactments of peoples, that is enactments of Assemblies of their republics. That right may be exercised only under conditions and in a manner which would be established pursuant to the SFRY constitution, with the consent of every people, and its republic, separately and all of them together. The unilateral proclamation of the Republic of Croatia as sovereign and independent in the view of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia is in violation of the provisions of the SFRY Constitution on the composition of the SFRY as a State community of the peoples of Yugoslavia, as well as on those on the borders of Yugoslavia as a Federal State and a State community of voluntarily united peoples and their republics. The Ministry of Defence of Yugoslavia sent information to the presidency of the SFRY, which discussed the problems that occurred and they came to the conclusion that, on the territory of the SFRY, in several places, there were secret imports of weapons that were made and they were being handed out to the population and that the laws and constitution of the Federal State were being grossly violated and that there is a danger of an uprising with unforeseeable consequences and conflicts -- could be an international conflict of limitless proportions .

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down? He is reading and the interpreters do not have a text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, no problem. A few minutes ago I said that it would take some time, so that is why I... The presidency of Yugoslavia issued an order saying that all armed formations would have to be disbanded throughout Yugoslavia -- these did not belong to the armed forces of Yugoslavia -- within a time limit of 10 days. In Article 5 of this order, it was stipulated that the Yugoslav People's Army would provide protection for all citizens throughout the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Soon, the first major incidents occurred. May I recall some of them? The Croat armed paramilitary forces, in the town of Pakrac which had a Serb population, attacked the municipal building and, in order to prevent an escalation, units of the Yugoslav People's Army were sent and fire was opened against them. At a meeting of the presidency of the SFRY, the Chief of Defence, General Veljko Kadijevic, informed the presidency of the fact that the measures envisaged in the order are not being implemented and he proposed that a state of emergency be introduced, which was rejected. After a new incident in the area of Plitvice and Titova Korinica, the presidency of the SFRY issued orders to the Yugoslav People's Army to ensure a cease-fire, to have it observed, and to raise the state of alert within the JNA to a higher level. At the beginning of the trial against Martin Spegelj, the organiser of the arms purchases, the building of the military court in Zagreb was attacked. New incidents occurred in Borovo Selo, Eastern Slavonia, Knin Krajina and after Croat paramilitary units attacked military facilities in Trogir and the military command ordered mobilisation and a higher state of alertness. You were in a position to see the attacks in Trogir yesterday. After the acts of secession made by Croatia and Slovenia, if we were to analyse the existing state of affairs, we could draw the conclusion that, in Yugoslavia, public order was seriously jeopardised. Also, that the Yugoslav People's Army, according to internal and international law, acquired the right to react appropriately. In this same way, the army has been acting in Turkey, Algeria and Northern Ireland, so if we were to analyse the existing state of affairs, as well as constitutional principles of Yugoslavia from 1974, the practice of states in similar situations, the Yugoslav People's Army had the right to try to stop secession, according to all international documents and according to the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On the basis of these theoretical opinions, and on the basis of an analysis of international documents, the international jurisprudence of the international court of law, according to practise in other countries and, finally, in keeping with the duties derived from the constitution, there is sufficient argument to bring in a conclusion as to whether the Yugoslav People's Army, on its own territory, acted as an aggressor, or did it act in conformity with international and internal law? The prevalent opinion is that we are talking about a reaction on the basis of legal documents and that the action was a legitimate action taken by the JNA. After a certain amount of time, it became evident that, on the territory of Yugoslavia, an internal conflict was being waged with unforeseeable consequences between the republics and peoples wishing to secede, and those republics and peoples and the Yugoslav People's Army, who wished to retain the unity of the Federal State. The Yugoslav People's Army acted according to all the arguments presented earlier on in keeping with the constitution and the Charter of the United Nations, and in the year 1991 was marked with a great number of casualties on both sides. In 1991, all the arguments presented indicate the fact that we were dealing with a conflict within one country and that country is the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that the conflict was between the peoples wishing to secede and the Yugoslav People's Army wishing to retain the Federal State. The Yugoslav Army acting in keeping with the constitution and the United Nations charter, had no other choice but to decide upon a solution to retain and safeguard the country. If we were to try and find arguments for an opinion which is contrary to that one, it would be difficult to do so, relying on any legal document, either international or domestic, and without prejudice, everything would lead us to conclude that, during the year 1991, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, a civil war took place and not an international conflict. The war was waged within the frontiers of Yugoslavia itself between its citizens with different political goals. Let us now pay attention to the legal arguments in this regard. An international conflict by definition takes place between States and an internal one between the citizens of one State, or parts of states, against the central powers and authorities that be. For us to be able to understand this more fully, that is to say, what we mean by an "international conflict" and what we mean by an "internal conflict", let me quote a fairly old concept on the character of warfare and a modern view. Riviere, in his book, "The Basis of International Law" dating back to 1898 underlined the following: The differences made between a real war, which is waged between states, and an international war and a civil war -- a war which is the subject of international law is only a war between states. A civil war is not a war which is the subject of international law. A Government has, before it rebels, insurgents which are to be treated as such, but it is up to that Government to have an attitude as if it were dealing with belligerent sides. As opposed to international conflicts in which the two warring parties are states, the warring parties are states, internal conflicts take place within a single State territory -- between antagonistic groups, citizens of that same State. The causes of internal conflict can be manifold -- class differences, national ones, religious or tribal. Along with this, internal conflicts can move within different time scopes. A completely new definition by the Vice-President of the International Law Association states that, in international conflicts, the conflicting parties are equal, which is a reflection of the sovereign equality of states, and their relationships and the rules of international law will be applied to their relationships. Internal conflicts, however, as they are waged in a territory over which legal authority has territorial supremacy, are waged between citizens over whom the State has personal supremacy and it logically transpires that internal conflicts come within the competence of the State itself. The use of force in order to change the existing state of affairs and the possible taking over of power for all legal systems in the world are qualified as criminal acts, regardless of the background and motives of the conflict in question. The legal Government, with its armed force, acts in Defence of its constitutional rights and the rebels are punished on the basis of criminal law. Therefore, if we wish to prove, or to note the facts according to which a court will be able to draw its own conclusions as to the character of a war, and the character of the war on the territory of former Yugoslavia as it was during the year 1991, in view of the critical date, that is to say, 20 November of that year, we must prove, prior to this, the warring parties on the territory of the former SFRY, that is to say, whether Croatia, at that particular moment, at that particular date of 20 November, whether Croatia was a State from the aspects of international law, or whether it was not. If it was a State, then it was an international conflict; if arguments show that it was not, then the contrary conclusion can be drawn and the conflict was not an international one -- it was an internal one. We have sufficient facts on the basis of which we are able to see that, in the course of 1991, a conflict was waged on the territory of Yugoslavia between peoples who wished to secede and those peoples who wished to retain the country's unity and the Yugoslav People's Army, which, as the guarantor of the sovereignty of the State according to the constitution, had to act in line with the constitution. Therefore, nothing that is against the law can have a legally respected consequence. Therefore, if Croatia was formed as a State contrary to the law, then it is quite certain that it cannot be recognised as a State in the course of 1991. For this reason, we are going to draw our attention to the legal arguments in this regard. How can we treat the stepping down of Croatia from Yugoslavia in the course of 1991 and onwards? Was this done in keeping with international and internal law, or was it not? If it was not, then we have on the scene, concerning Croatia's recognition, some other factors -- not legal factors, that is to say, political factors which should not interest this Tribunal. We are going to base our assumptions only on legal arguments for this particular purpose. The secession of certain republics from the makeup of Yugoslavia, the advocates of the Federal State, treat it as an act of secession and the representatives of the republics which step down treated this as an act of self-determination. If you step down from a State, it breaks up the unity of that same State. On the other hand, speaking about the principle of self-determination, it can be explained in different ways. That is why we are going to try to show, on the basis of the theory of international law and the jurisprudence of the International Court of Law, to give an answer to the following question: in the case of Croatia stepping down from Yugoslavia, was it an act of secession, or was it an act of self-determination? In theory, that is the theory of international law, the principle of self-determination can be explained as a request to answer to the desire of peoples who, due to historical conditions, were not able to create a State of their own. The United Nations charter, in article 1.2 stresses the following: "The development of friendly relations among nations, based on a respect for the principles of equality and self-determination of nations and the undertaking of corresponding measures in order to strengthen general peace." Article 55 underlines the following: "With the aim of creating conditions of stability and well-being, which are indispensable for peaceful and friendly relationships among nations, based on a respect for the principles of equality and self-determination of peoples, the United Nations worked towards, et cetera." For a long time, in theory, in the theory of law, a debate was waged over the question of the notion of self-determination itself. Some people maintained that it was a political and others that it was a legal issue. So, for example, (INAUDIBLE) advocates the view that it is a political issue, whereas Wright and Duncan maintain that it is a legal question. Self-determination as a political principle appeared at the time of the American and French revolutions and the doctrine and practice of international law of the modern times sees self-determination as a component part of the democratic changes and view it as part of the struggle against pressure and not the idea of separatism. The league of nations rejected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, could you please come to the point -- speak about self-determination in Croatia without citing the legal references. We do have two written documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honours, you need not repeat what has been written, but move to the question you have been asked: why you consider it to be an internal conflict and not an international one, because both sides have read the document. So there is no need to repeat it -- what is your opinion, why you consider that to be so and that is all that you are being asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us now dwell on the problem of Croatia alone. Did Croatia, in 1991, on 20 November, exist as a State from the aspects of international law, or did it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it or was it not a State and that is the only thing that is relevant in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the international community, in international relations, in the theory and practice of international law, for an entity to be a State, it must fulfil three elements -- territory, population and a sovereign authority -- Government. Let us look at all these three elements in the question of Croatia. Therefore, territory: Croatia had a territory which was bounded by administrative and not international frontiers. Secondly, the population of this territory: in Croatia, you had Croats and Serbs living in the Republic. There were more than 12 per cent of Serbs living there. Therefore, a population which at that moment was divided -- the Croats came out in favour of stepping down from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On the other hand, the Serb people came out in favour of remaining in a unified Federal State. Therefore, we had a population which expressed completely different views as to Croatia's unity and, finally, we come to the most important element and that is sovereign Government. For a given State to say that it is a State, it must have a clearly defined territory with international frontiers; it must have a permanent population and not a nomad population, and finally it must have a sovereign authority, sovereign power and authority or Government. What do we mean by sovereign authority? It is the supreme authority over the given territory and population. What do we mean by "supreme power and authority over a given territory and population"? It is that power and authority which can have effective administrative control over that particular territory and that particular population. Let us take a look at that point. Could Croatia exercise effective administrative control over its entire territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you stick to 1991, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am -- we are talking about the year 1991. Did the Croat legislation, for example -- was it applied in Knin, in Eastern and Western Slavonia? No, it was not. Did the military police from Croatia, from Zagreb -- could the police from Zagreb come to Knin territory to arrest somebody? It could not. Did the court -- was the court able, from Zagreb, to set up its power and authority in Knin? It could not. Why? Because Croatia did not have sovereign power and authority over its territory -- entire territory. Let us now take a look at how international theory, jurisprudence, looks at States which do not have sovereign power and authority. When it comes to the Aland Islands and I will quote: "The question of Finland arose --" Please follow what I am saying. In its opinion, the commission referred to the question of defining the sovereign authority as an indispensable requirement for the constitution of Finland as a sovereign State. Certain elements which are essential for the existence -- crucial for the existence -- of a State were lacking in a given period. The political and social life was disorganised. The authorities were not sufficiently powerful to be able to confirm their power and authority, and especially important, the civilian war was raging. The Government was banished and forcibly prevented from performing its duties and now we come to the conclusion: "It is difficult to say on what date the Finnish republic was constituted as a State in the legal sense of the word. At all events, it was not the case before a stable political organisation was set up, nor was it before the public authorities became sufficiently powerful to be able to protect themselves throughout the country's territory without the help of foreign troops." Therefore, a relevant international commission concluded, in this instance, that if the State -- or an entity pleading to be a State -- cannot or is unable to control its entire territory, it cannot be considered a State from the aspects of international law. Now let us move on further. The acts on the proclamation of independence of Croatia and Slovenia and the ruling of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia were declared unconstitutional and, therefore, it was proclaimed that they were not in line with the constitution and, therefore, legally, not complying with the constitution. Now let us move on further. On 29 November 1991, that is to say, after the critical date, the Badinter Commission -- I imagine that we will be discussing this Commission later -- stresses in its opinion number 1, although, until now the SFRY has retained its international nature, that is to say, that in its opinion the commission states that Yugoslavia is still a subject of international law, that is to say, that it exists, so if Yugoslavia exists, then, on the same territory, there cannot be two States. Another conclusion: the recourse to force has led to armed conflict -- I especially draw your attention to this -- between the different elements of the federation. So, it is stated quite clearly here that, in 1991, on 29 November, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there was an internal conflict between the members of the federation. Further on, if we have a look at how the authorities and Federal agencies of Yugoslavia were operating, until the end of November, or more precisely until 5 December, the Federal State, namely, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was headed by a Croat. Tell me, is there a State which is at war with another State and, at the same time, the citizen of this other State is its President? The Minister of Defence was a Croat. The Federal Prime Minister was a Croat. The Minister of Foreign Affairs was also a Croat. Therefore, the representatives of Croatia took part in the work of the Federal authorities. Stipe Mesic was withdrawn on 5 December, but all the rest remained. So, if the representatives of Croatia take part in the work of the Federal authorities, how can this be interpreted? If we suppose that Yugoslavia is a State, can it be at war with Croatia if we suppose that it is a State and if the citizens of the country with which it is at war hold all the key positions in that country? So, what was it all about? It was about the following: in Yugoslavia, in 1991, there was still a struggle going on to maintain the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. I wish to remind you of the statement made by the President of the United States of America in 1945. He stated that those countries which are the founding members of the United Nations, their territorial integrity and sovereignty has to be particularly respected. Therefore, in 1991, Yugoslavia was still trying to maintain its unity and territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I am afraid we have to stop at 5 past 1 and I wonder whether you need more time, or have you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I need about 15 minutes more or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Go on, until 1.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUKALOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible. It is very interesting to note the official position of the United States of America. Mr. Baker has underlined the following: the fact that Slovenia and Croatia unilaterally proclaimed independence, regardless of all warnings, they resorted to force in order to grab their borders and this actually caused a civil conflict and we had suggested that this was going to happen. Further on, what can be of interest is the following: to answer the following question, who qualifies the conflict on the territory of a certain State? What is the organ that is supposed to do this? This has to be done by the Security Council. Let us see how the Security Council behaved. The Security Council resolution 713, dated 25 September 1991, has emphasised the following: "Deeply concerned over the conflicts in Yugoslavia." So, the Security Council is speaking of conflicts on the territory of Yugoslavia. Security Council resolution 721: "Deeply concerned over the conflict in Yugoslavia." That was on 27 November. The Security Council, in all its statements, adheres to the following notion: that the conflict is taking place on the territory of Yugoslavia, so, if the Security Council says that the conflict is being waged on the territory of Yugoslavia, and that is the body that is in charge of international peace and security and the only one that can qualify a conflict, if that is so, there are no arguments that can indicate that the war in Yugoslavia in 1991 and, in particular, on the critical date of 20 November 1991, was in an international conflict -- no. Finally, the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the draft Statute, says that an act cannot be considered to be an act of an aggression for the purposes of this Statute if the Security Council has not previously ascertained that a State has committed an act of aggression. The Security Council, in its resolutions, speaks about Yugoslavia -- about a conflict on the territory of Yugoslavia. Therefore, if a conflict is being waged on the territory of one State, between its citizens, and if the Security Council does not qualify it as an international conflict, and if Croatia does not have a single one of the attributes needed for recognition, then all of this points to the following conclusion, that the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1991, in view of the critical date of 20 November 1991, was an internal conflict. I really wanted to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one more thing. You omitted to mention Badinter's opinions. Perhaps a sentence or two on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I tried to shorten my remarks, because I was cautioned to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Actually, you did mention the opinion number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 29 November, I did, but I probably did refer to the one that you are interested in. I do not know if I can find it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think it is number 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is treatment of the proclamations of independence of Slovenia and Croatia. Here it is -- number 11 of the 16th. The situation is the same as regards the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia -- both proclaimed their independence on 25 June 1991 and this was suspended on 7 July 1991 for three months, as envisaged by the Brioni Declaration. According to this declaration, the suspension was to remain in force until 8 October 1991, when the two republics became sovereign according to international law. Let us analyse this. This was on 16 July. On 29 November, that is to say, a few months after, the Badinter Commission had underlined the following and the Badinter recommendations are not compulsory by nature, that Croatia and Slovenia became sovereign States. It gave an explanation on 29 November 1991, and it reads as follows: "Acts of independence can be treated and I quote `only as a republic expressing its will to be independent'." So, this one-sided proclamation of independence by a State is irrelevant from the point of view of international law. By a unilateral act, a country, a State, can qualify a certain conflict, make a statement, renounce a certain right, set the date and hour on which a blockade would be imposed, but it cannot unilaterally proclaim its independence from the point of view of international law -- this is quite irrelevant. If this position is to be accepted, the rulings of this court will have far-reaching consequences. If a State can be established by unilateral acts, what will happen in one of the following periods? Depending on political interests, there will be disintegration of States and, therefore, political chaos and, on the other hand, this will be a flagrant violation of the basic objectives of the Charter and that is the creation of a world in which future generations will be saved from the horrors of war, where belief in basic human rights, and where there will be social prosperity, will be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Since this has been mentioned this morning, on the territory of Kosovo, was there any such proclamation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a brief explanation: on the territory of Kosovo, we have a similar situation. The international community has spoken in favour of the unity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is the year 1998 -- eight years ago, part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, rather a part of Serbia, where the Albanian national minority lives, unilaterally declared its independence. This independence was not confirmed by anyone. Everyone absolutely rejected this, but what will happen if, tomorrow, a possibility arises of introducing some kind of retroactive recognition of the Republic of Kosovo and then the acts that are committed by the army are proclaimed to be international conflicts? This is not the only case. Chechnya also proclaimed its independence, but no-one in the world qualified this as an international conflict between Russia and Chechnya. What will happen if tomorrow Northern Ireland, Corsica and the Basque and others do the same? So, on this particular matter the court takes the position that, by an unilateral act, one can proclaim one's statehood, the decisions of this court will have very dangerous consequences for the 21st century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you are referring to our court, it is for us to follow. We do not follow policy considerations. We base our decisions only on law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you through? I wonder if you have any questions to put tomorrow in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will stand adjourned until tomorrow. (At 1.20 p.m. the matter adjourned until Thursday, 23 April 1998 at 8.30 a.m.)
